s001.text: UPSC, twenty eighteen. Geography optional, Paper One, twenty marks. Explain the origin, progress and retreat of the Indian monsoon, and discuss its impact on the Indian economy. The easy answer opens with one cause. Our own Class Eleven textbook warns against exactly that.

s002.text: And this idea keeps coming back. In the last eleven sittings, UPSC asked about the monsoon in seven. So let's learn to write this one well. Then its cousins get easier.

s003.text: First, read what it asks. Explain means show how and why. Discuss means weigh more than one effect. And there are four jobs: origin, progress, retreat, and the economy. Miss one, and the answer has a hole.

s004.text: Start with the easy origin story. In summer, land heats faster than the sea. A low forms over the hot north-west. Moist sea air flows in, and it rains. That part is true.

s005.text: But our Class Eleven book adds a warning. No single theory has fully explained the monsoon. And the record shows why. India is hotter in May than in July, yet the heavy rain waits for July.

s006.text: So scientists now picture something bigger. Near the equator sits a belt of rising air and rain. It follows the sun north each summer.

s007.text: By July it lies at about twenty to twenty-five degrees north, as the monsoon trough. The monsoon is that rain belt arriving, not a giant sea breeze.

s008.text: Other parts work with it. Winds from the southern Indian Ocean cross the equator and swing to the south-west.

s009.text: A fast low-level jet carries them past Somalia to our west coast. High above, an easterly jet sets in.

s010.text: Now we write. There is no word limit, so we set our own: about three hundred words in fourteen minutes. Open with one line that defines the monsoon and shows the stakes.

s011.text: Origin gets the classic theories, each with its author. Halley's thermal concept. Flohn's dynamic concept, the shifting rain belt. Koteswaram's Tibetan heating, with the jet above. Then the Somali jet, and one line on El Niño. Underline the terms an examiner scans for.

s012.text: Now the diagram. Give it about a minute. India, the high below the equator, and arrows bending north-east. Mark the heat low, the trough, and the two branches.

s013.text: Progress is dates and directions. The Andaman Sea about the twenty-second of May. Kerala about the first of June. The whole country by about the eighth of July. That date is IMD's newer normal. Many older notes still say the fifteenth.

s014.text: Retreat starts in the north-west around the seventeenth of September. Most of India is clear by the fifteenth of October. Then the winds turn, and Tamil Nadu gets its north-east monsoon.

s015.text: The last job is the one people rush. The economy needs figures, not one line. Nearly half of Indians work in farming. Nearly half of that farming depends on rain. Kharif crops give almost half the year's grain. A good monsoon fills the reservoirs. And a weak one shows up in prices. This October, the Reserve Bank named the deficient monsoon as a pressure on food prices.

s016.text: End where the science is going. June to September rain has fallen about six percent in fifty years. Wet spells have grown more intense. So better forecasts and stored water are India's insurance.

s017.text: Now put it beside the easy answer. One cause. An old date. Vague on the retreat. One line on the economy. No diagram. Both took fourteen minutes. Only one did all four jobs.

s018.text: And here is the payoff. The same frame answers its cousins. Twenty twenty asked for the factors behind the monsoon. Twenty twenty-two asked why it is unpredictable. Twenty nineteen asked why it is erratic. Learn the frame once. To see why the rain belt moves, watch our monsoon episode.
